subject: anatomy
topic: Shoulder suspension, capsule and stabilizers
prompt: After an acromioclavicular injury, the trapezoid and acromioclavicular ligaments are torn but the conoid remains intact. Which residual mechanical behavior is most consistent with this pattern?

options.text: The coracoid can rotate around a remaining vertical conoid fulcrum
The coracoid remains fixed because the trapezoid chiefly resists distraction
The intact conoid chiefly prevents anteroposterior translation, so horizontal stability is fully preserved
The torn trapezoid eliminates vertical suspension completely despite an intact conoid

explanation: The conoid remains an almost vertical, posteromedial restraint to distraction; loss of the trapezoid permits rotation around it.

distractorExplanations.B: The conoid, rather than the trapezoid alone, is the major vertical distraction restraint.
distractorExplanations.C: The AC capsular ligaments are the principal anteroposterior restraints. An intact conoid does not restore their lost horizontal stability.
distractorExplanations.D: The conoid remains a major vertical distraction restraint and can serve as a fulcrum; its preservation is not equivalent to complete coracoclavicular disruption.

learningObjective: Predict residual acromioclavicular mechanics after selective conoid, trapezoid and capsular injuries.

subject: anatomy
topic: Shoulder suspension, capsule and stabilizers
prompt: Stress testing shows excessive anteroposterior translation at the acromioclavicular joint but near-normal vertical suspension of the scapula. Which injury best fits?

options.text: Coracohumeral ligament damaged with acromioclavicular ligaments preserved
Acromioclavicular capsular ligaments damaged with coracoclavicular ligaments preserved
Conoid and trapezoid damaged with acromioclavicular ligaments preserved
Costoclavicular ligament damaged with acromioclavicular ligaments preserved

explanation: Acromioclavicular ligaments provide the greatest resistance to anteroposterior translation; intact coracoclavicular ligaments retain much of the vertical suspension.

distractorExplanations.A: The coracohumeral ligament stabilizes the glenohumeral joint, not the acromioclavicular articulation.
distractorExplanations.C: This chiefly compromises vertical translation and rotation rather than producing isolated anteroposterior laxity.
distractorExplanations.D: This alters the medial clavicular fulcrum at the sternoclavicular region.

learningObjective: Distinguish horizontal acromioclavicular instability from failure of vertical coracoclavicular suspension.

subject: anatomy
topic: Shoulder suspension, capsule and stabilizers
prompt: An intra-articular fibrocartilaginous structure is detached from the posterosuperior medial clavicle and from the first costal cartilage near the sternum. Which joint function is most directly compromised?

options.text: Suspension of the scapula from the lateral clavicle
Retention of the biceps tendon within the intertubercular groove
Partition and soft-tissue stability of the sternoclavicular joint
Deepening of the glenoid socket

explanation: The sternoclavicular disc attaches at these sites, divides the cavity and contributes stability despite limited bony congruence.

Middle and inferior glenohumeral ligaments only
Coracoacromial and superior transverse scapular ligaments
Coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments

topic: Shoulder suspension, capsule and stabilizers
prompt: During a shoulder arthrogram, contrast exits through the normal anterior capsular opening below the coracoid and surrounds the upper border of subscapularis. Which interpretation best fits the anatomy?

The contrast proves that the supraspinatus tendon has ruptured
Filling of the subacromial bursa is an obligatory normal continuation of the glenohumeral cavity
Any contrast outside the fibrous joint capsule necessarily proves a pathological rupture

explanation: The anterior opening below the coracoid connects the joint cavity to a bursa around the upper border of subscapularis.

subject: anatomy
topic: Branch-level localization in the shoulder and arm
prompt: External rotation is weak and infraspinatus is denervated, but supraspinatus contraction is preserved. Which location best explains an isolated suprascapular neuropathy with this pattern?

options.text: Within the quadrangular space
At the lateral border of the scapular spine after the supraspinatus branches
At the upper trunk before the suprascapular nerve arises
At the suprascapular notch before entry into the supraspinous fossa

explanation: The nerve supplies supraspinatus before curving around the scapular spine to infraspinatus.

subject: anatomy
topic: Branch-level localization in the shoulder and arm
prompt: After a focal posterior-wall axillary injury, teres major and the lower part of subscapularis are weak, while latissimus dorsi and deltoid are preserved. Which branch is most likely interrupted?

options.text: Thoracodorsal nerve
Axillary nerve
Lower subscapular nerve
Upper subscapular nerve

explanation: The lower subscapular nerve supplies lower subscapularis and usually teres major; separate thoracodorsal and axillary branches remain functional.

distractorExplanations.A: This supplies latissimus dorsi, which is preserved.
distractorExplanations.B: This supplies deltoid and teres minor, not teres major.
distractorExplanations.D: It enters subscapularis high and does not usually supply teres major.

subject: anatomy
topic: Branch-level localization in the shoulder and arm
prompt: A branch crossing anterior to the axillary vessels is divided where it pierces clavipectoral fascia. Pectoralis major loses part of its innervation, but musculocutaneous motor function remains normal. Which localization is best?

options.text: Lateral cord before all its branches
Medial pectoral nerve within pectoralis minor
Thoracodorsal nerve on the posterior axillary wall
Lateral pectoral nerve after it leaves the lateral cord

explanation: The lateral pectoral nerve crosses the vessels, pierces clavipectoral fascia and reaches pectoralis major. A distal branch injury spares musculocutaneous function.

distractorExplanations.A: This would also threaten musculocutaneous function and the lateral contribution to the median nerve.
distractorExplanations.B: That nerve approaches and supplies pectoralis minor before continuing to major; it is not the described fascial branch.

subject: anatomy
topic: Branch-level localization in the shoulder and arm
prompt: A lesion confined to the anterior branch of the axillary nerve weakens the anterior deltoid. Which preserved finding would best support that localization rather than injury of the entire axillary trunk?

options.text: Teres minor contraction with sensation over the usual upper lateral cutaneous territory
Normal supraspinatus contraction alone
Normal triceps contraction alone
Normal latissimus dorsi contraction alone

explanation: The posterior axillary branch gives the nerve to teres minor and the upper lateral cutaneous nerve, so these may remain intact.

distractorExplanations.B: Supraspinatus is supplied by the suprascapular nerve and can be normal even after an entire axillary lesion.
distractorExplanations.C: Triceps is supplied by the radial nerve and does not distinguish anterior-branch from whole-axillary injury.
distractorExplanations.D: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus and lies outside the axillary nerve.

learningObjective: Distinguish anterior axillary-branch injury from injury of the whole axillary nerve.

subject: anatomy
topic: Branch-level localization in the shoulder and arm
prompt: A small penetrating wound lateral to the biceps tendon causes anterolateral forearm numbness. Biceps and brachialis retain normal power. Which structure is most consistent with the lesion?

options.text: Medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm
Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm after the motor branches have arisen
Musculocutaneous nerve before it enters coracobrachialis
Superficial radial nerve beneath brachioradialis

explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve continues as this cutaneous branch after supplying arm muscles and passes lateral to the biceps tendon.

topic: Elbow stability and forearm load transfer
prompt: A radial-head fracture is accompanied by distal radioulnar instability. Under axial load the radius migrates proximally. Which additional lesion best unifies the findings?

Isolated rupture of the bicipital aponeurosis
Disruption of the interosseous membrane
Isolated annular-ligament laxity with the interosseous membrane intact

explanation: The radial head, interosseous membrane and distal radioulnar joint are linked longitudinal stabilizers; their combined disruption defines the Essex-Lopresti pattern.

distractorExplanations.B: This anterior fascial injury does not account for radial migration and distal radioulnar dissociation.

Annular ligament alone
Distal radioulnar articular disc alone
Anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament complex

explanation: The anterior ulnar collateral band is the major valgus restraint; an intact complex can maintain stability when the radial head is lost.

subject: anatomy
topic: Elbow stability and forearm load transfer
prompt: Two equal-sized tears involve the triangular fibrocartilage: one is central and one peripheral. Why does the central lesion have less intrinsic vascular support for repair?

options.text: Only the outer part of the disc has a substantial blood supply
The central disc has a denser direct capillary network but receives less synovial diffusion
The peripheral disc is avascular, while vessels reach the center through the ulnar articular surface
Both locations have equally abundant intrinsic vessels, so tear position cannot affect vascular support

explanation: Gray describes vascularization of approximately the outer 15-20% of the disc, with the remaining central portion avascular.

distractorExplanations.B: The central disc is largely avascular; reduced intrinsic vascular support is not caused by having more central capillaries.
distractorExplanations.C: This reverses the vascular gradient: regional arterial branches supply the outer part, while the central disc is avascular.

subject: anatomy
topic: Elbow stability and forearm load transfer
prompt: With the ulna approximately fixed, imaging tracks pronation. Which paired movement is expected?

options.text: The proximal radius moves medial to the ulna and the distal radius stays lateral
Radial head spins proximally while the distal radius and hand swing around the ulnar head
Ulnar head rotates around a stationary distal radius while the radial head stays immobile
Both radius and ulna rotate as a rigid unit solely at the radiocarpal joint

explanation: The two radioulnar pivot joints act together: proximal radial rotation accompanies a distal arc around the ulna.

distractorExplanations.A: During pronation the proximal radius remains lateral while its distal end crosses anteromedially.
distractorExplanations.C: This reverses the dominant relative motion when the ulna is fixed.
distractorExplanations.D: Forearm rotation primarily occurs at the radioulnar joints, not solely at the wrist.

subject: anatomy
topic: Elbow stability and forearm load transfer
prompt: A patient has weak rapid, resisted supination with the elbow flexed, but can still perform slow unresisted supination with the elbow extended. Which muscle's loss best explains the disproportionate deficit?

options.text: Supinator
Brachioradialis
Biceps brachii
Pronator quadratus

explanation: Biceps contributes especially to rapid or resisted supination in flexion, while supinator can support slow unresisted rotation in extension.

distractorExplanations.A: Supinator supports slow unresisted supination, especially in extension; loss of biceps better explains the disproportionate deficit during rapid resisted supination in elbow flexion.
distractorExplanations.B: Brachioradialis primarily flexes the elbow and can bring the forearm toward mid-position; it is not the principal forceful supinator in the stated flexed-elbow test.
distractorExplanations.D: It pronates the forearm and cannot explain selective loss of forceful supination.

learningObjective: Use load and elbow position to distinguish contributions to supination.

subject: anatomy
topic: Forearm vessels and nerve relationships
prompt: Contrast in the inferior ulnar collateral artery crosses to the ulnar arterial system anterior to the medial epicondyle. Which returning branch completes this direct anastomosis?

options.text: Posterior ulnar recurrent artery
Posterior interosseous recurrent artery
Radial recurrent artery
Anterior ulnar recurrent artery

explanation: It ascends between brachialis and pronator teres to join the inferior ulnar collateral artery anterior to the epicondyle.

distractorExplanations.A: This ascends behind the medial epicondyle, deep to flexor carpi ulnaris.
distractorExplanations.B: This reaches the posterolateral elbow deep to anconeus and joins the middle collateral route.

learningObjective: Trace an anterior medial-epicondylar arterial collateral route.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice

subject: anatomy
topic: Forearm vessels and nerve relationships
prompt: A vessel leaves the common interosseous artery, passes between the oblique cord and proximal border of the interosseous membrane, then descends with the deep radial branch. Which vessel and compartment are involved?

options.text: Posterior interosseous artery in the posterior forearm
Anterior interosseous artery in the anterior forearm
Radial recurrent artery in the anterior forearm
Superior ulnar collateral artery in the posterior forearm

explanation: This is the proximal posterior route; the artery accompanies the posterior interosseous nerve among the extensor muscles.

distractorExplanations.C: It ascends toward the lateral elbow rather than descending through this proximal interosseous interval.
distractorExplanations.D: It accompanies the ulnar nerve around the medial elbow, not the posterior interosseous nerve.

learningObjective: Follow the posterior interosseous artery through the proximal membrane interval.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice

subject: anatomy
topic: Forearm vessels and nerve relationships
prompt: The median nerve crosses superficial to the ulnar artery in the proximal forearm. What usually lies between these two structures at their crossing?

options.text: Tendon of brachioradialis
Ulnar head of pronator teres
Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris
Bicipital aponeurosis

explanation: The median nerve passes between the pronator heads and is separated from the ulnar artery by the ulnar head.

distractorExplanations.A: Brachioradialis overlies the radial pathway laterally.
distractorExplanations.C: This is part of the medial ulnar-nerve entrance to the forearm.
distractorExplanations.D: This covers the cubital fossa superficial to the brachial artery and median nerve rather than separating this forearm crossing.

learningObjective: Identify the muscular partition between median nerve and ulnar artery.

subject: anatomy
topic: Forearm vessels and nerve relationships
prompt: After compression at the distal border of supinator, finger extension fails but wrist extension persists with radial deviation. Cutaneous sensation is normal. Which explanation best fits?

options.text: The superficial radial branch has been interrupted while the deep motor branch is intact
An isolated ulnar lesion denervates extensor carpi ulnaris and the finger extensors
Digital extensors and extensor carpi ulnaris are denervated while proximal radial wrist-extensor branches are spared
A radial-trunk lesion above all wrist-extensor branches has removed every radial wrist-extensor contribution

explanation: The distal deep radial pathway supplies digital extensors and extensor carpi ulnaris. Preserved radial wrist extensors extend the wrist with an unopposed radial component.

distractorExplanations.A: A superficial branch lesion would chiefly affect cutaneous sensation, not cause the stated digital-extensor and extensor-carpi-ulnaris deficit.
distractorExplanations.B: These extensor muscles receive radial/posterior interosseous innervation, not ulnar motor fibers.
distractorExplanations.D: Such a complete proximal lesion would not preserve the observed wrist extension. The retained radial wrist extensors support a distal deep-branch localization.

learningObjective: Explain preserved radially deviated wrist extension in a distal deep-radial lesion.

Posterior interosseous-nerve division within supinator
Musculocutaneous-nerve division in the axilla
A branch of the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm crossing the incision

distractorExplanations.A: This would impair ulnar hand motor function and digital sensation.
distractorExplanations.B: This causes extensor motor deficits rather than medial forearm cutaneous loss.

learningObjective: Distinguish medial forearm cutaneous injury from ulnar nerve injury.

subject: anatomy
topic: Finger and thumb tendon mechanics
prompt: Following forced flexion of an extended fingertip, active DIP extension is lost but passive extension is full. Months later the PIP joint hyperextends. What sequence best explains the progression?

options.text: Terminal extensor disruption allows proximal migration of the extensor apparatus, increasing its PIP extension moment
Central-slip disruption moves the lateral bands palmar to the PIP axis
Flexor digitorum profundus avulsion initially prevents DIP flexion
A1 pulley thickening initially locks the entire digit in flexion

explanation: A mallet lesion removes distal restraint. The remaining extensor apparatus can migrate proximally and contribute to secondary swan-neck deformity.

distractorExplanations.B: That produces PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension, the opposite later posture.
distractorExplanations.C: This would primarily abolish active DIP flexion, not extension.
distractorExplanations.D: Triggering at the flexor sheath does not explain the isolated initial DIP extensor failure.

learningObjective: Explain secondary PIP hyperextension following terminal extensor disruption.

subject: anatomy
topic: Finger and thumb tendon mechanics
prompt: After a dorsal PIP laceration, a finger initially extends weakly. Later the PIP rests flexed while the DIP hyperextends. Which change converts the lateral extensor bands into PIP flexors?

options.text: Dorsal migration of the lateral bands while the central slip remains intact
Palmar migration of the lateral bands past the PIP axis after central-slip failure
Proximal migration of an intact terminal tendon after distal-phalanx avulsion
Palmar migration of intact lateral bands caused solely by rupture of the terminal insertion at the DIP

explanation: With central-slip failure and attenuation of the triangular ligament, the lateral bands move volarly; they flex the PIP while the tightened terminal mechanism still extends the DIP.

distractorExplanations.C: That mechanism favors mallet-related swan-neck posture, with PIP hyperextension.
distractorExplanations.D: Terminal extensor failure initially causes mallet finger and may lead to PIP hyperextension; it does not reproduce the stated central-slip-driven sequence.

learningObjective: Relate central-slip failure to lateral-band migration and boutonniere posture.

subject: anatomy
topic: Finger and thumb tendon mechanics
prompt: After forced radial deviation of the thumb MCP joint, its torn ulnar collateral ligament lies superficial to the adductor aponeurosis. Why is direct ligament healing impeded?

options.text: The displaced ligament remains beneath the aponeurosis and directly opposed to its phalangeal insertion
The entire failure is due to loss of blood supply, even when the torn ends remain directly opposed
The adductor aponeurosis is interposed between the avulsed ligament and its distal attachment
The adductor aponeurosis pulls the torn ligament into its attachment site and permanently tightens it

explanation: A Stener lesion displaces the torn ligament around the free edge of the adductor aponeurosis, which prevents apposition to its insertion.

distractorExplanations.A: The stated superficial displacement means the aponeurosis intervenes, so direct apposition is not preserved.
distractorExplanations.B: The defining anatomical obstacle is soft-tissue interposition preventing apposition; global loss of blood supply is not required.
distractorExplanations.D: The aponeurosis instead separates the displaced ligament from its insertion; it does not automatically restore and tighten the repair interface.

learningObjective: Explain impaired healing when adductor aponeurosis intervenes in a thumb UCL tear.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy: The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice

subject: anatomy
topic: Finger and thumb tendon mechanics
prompt: During reconstruction of a finger flexor sheath, which pair of pulleys is most important to retain to limit bowstringing along the proximal and middle phalanges?

options.text: A1 and A3
A3 and A5
C1 and C2
A2 and A4

explanation: A2 overlies the proximal phalanx and A4 the middle phalanx; these are the key finger pulleys resisting flexor bowstringing.

learningObjective: Identify the critical digital annular pulleys for preventing bowstringing.

MCP collaterals tighten in extension and are slack in flexion
Both joints have equally slack collateral ligaments in extension
The digital extensors abduct the finger only when the MCP is flexed

explanation: The changing metacarpal-head width gives position-dependent MCP collateral tension; PIP collateral restraint is maintained through flexion and extension.

distractorExplanations.D: MCP abduction is limited in full flexion by ligament tension and chiefly uses intrinsic muscles.

Into the common digital-flexor sheath at the wrist
